body:
Why nuclear safety is necessary

Nuclear fission releases useful energy, but reactor fuel and some materials produced during reactor operation are radioactive. Radioactivity is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable atomic nucleus, often accompanied by the emission of ionising radiation.

Ionising radiation can transfer enough energy to matter to remove electrons from atoms or molecules. Excessive radiation exposure can harm living tissue. Nuclear safety therefore seeks to protect workers, the public and the environment during ordinary operation and possible abnormal events.

Two ideas must be distinguished. Radiation exposure means being exposed to radiation. Radioactive contamination means that radioactive material is present on a surface, in an object or inside a living body where it is not intended to be. Exposure does not, by itself, mean that a person has become contaminated.

Defence in depth

Defence in depth means using several complementary levels of prevention, protection and emergency preparedness, rather than depending on a single safety measure.

The basic safety functions of a nuclear power plant can be understood through 3 requirements:

  • Control the nuclear reaction: the reactor must be capable of being shut down safely when required.
  • Remove heat: cooling must be maintained as necessary, including after shutdown when decay heat remains.
  • Confine radioactive material: physical barriers and containment arrangements help prevent uncontrolled releases.

These functions are supported by operating procedures, monitoring, backup arrangements and trained personnel. If one protective measure becomes unavailable, other measures can help maintain safety.

Ordinary operation and emergency conditions

Radiation protection is needed during both ordinary operation and abnormal conditions. Under controlled operation, radioactive materials and any authorised releases are managed under specified safety requirements and monitored for compliance.

An abnormal event does not automatically mean that radioactive material has been released outside the installation. The appropriate emergency classification depends on the actual or potential consequences of the event.

Who operates, regulates and monitors?

OrganisationPrimary responsibility
NPCILOperates the nuclear-power plant and implements its safety arrangements.
AERBEstablishes and enforces nuclear and radiation-safety requirements and reviews compliance.
BARC Environmental Survey LaboratoriesConduct independent environmental radiological surveillance around nuclear sites.

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) is India's nuclear and radiation-safety regulator. It is different from NPCIL, which operates Kakrapar's power reactors.

The Environmental Survey Laboratories (ESLs) of BARC conduct environmental monitoring, including examination of air, water and soil. Their findings are submitted for regulatory review. Such measurements help establish environmental conditions, detect changes and assess whether radiation-protection arrangements are adequate.

Environmental monitoring is not the same as waiting for an accident to occur. It provides information during normal operation as well as a reference against which unusual measurements can be evaluated.

A nuclear-power station having emergency arrangements does not mean it is experiencing an emergency. Preparedness is a preventive requirement, and environmental surveillance is a continuing safety activity.

Prelims focus

  • Defence in depth uses multiple complementary protective measures.
  • The 3 basic safety functions are reaction control, heat removal and confinement of radioactive material.
  • NPCIL is the operator; AERB is the nuclear-safety regulator.
  • BARC ESLs conduct independent environmental radiological surveillance.
  • Environmental monitoring includes air, water and soil.
  • Trap: Radiation exposure and radioactive contamination are related but different concepts.

[Sources: Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Nuclear Power Plants, section on safety principles and emergency preparedness, consulted 16 November 2026; AERB, Radiation Safety for Protecting the Environment, sections on regulatory review and Environmental Survey Laboratories, consulted 16 November 2026; NPCIL and National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Environmental Impact Assessment Report for Kakrapar Atomic Power Project 3&4, Chapter 2, section 2.1, p. 2-2.]

pictures.alt: Three linked safety functions protect the reactor: safe shutdown, continued cooling and confinement. Cooling and confinement remain essential after shutdown.
pictures.caption: Reactor safety depends on controlling reactions, removing heat and confining radioactive material.

title: Nuclear safety at Kakrapar: protective systems and radiation monitoring

body:
Why emergency plans are prepared

Nuclear-power plants are designed and operated with protective systems, but emergency plans are also required because the possibility of an abnormal event cannot be treated as absolutely zero. An emergency plan specifies responsibilities, communication arrangements and protective measures that can be implemented if necessary.

Emergency classification considers the extent and potential consequences of an event. The classification helps determine whether plant personnel alone can manage the situation or whether wider authorities must undertake protective actions.

Plant, site and off-site emergencies

Emergency categoryArea of concernMain response responsibility
Plant emergencyConsequences are confined to the affected plant area.Plant management
Site emergencyConsequences may extend beyond one plant area but remain within the nuclear site.Site or plant management
Off-site emergencyActual or projected consequences may require protective action in the public domain outside the site.District authorities coordinate public-domain response with technical support from the plant.

A plant emergency does not automatically require evacuation of neighbouring villages. Similarly, the declaration or consideration of an off-site emergency need not mean that widespread radioactive contamination has already occurred. Protective decisions can be based on the possibility of exposure as well as measurements of an actual release.

The AERB reviews nuclear-power-plant emergency preparedness. Plant and site emergency plans are reviewed and approved by AERB. Off-site emergency plans are reviewed by AERB and approved by the responsible district or local authority.

Planning zones around a nuclear-power plant

India's nuclear siting and emergency-planning framework distinguishes areas according to their functions. These zones are designed for land-use control, preparedness and environmental monitoring. They are not automatic predictions of how far radiation will travel during an accident.

ZoneGeneral distance or extentPurpose
Exclusion zoneNot less than 1 km from each reactor centre for an NPP under the cited siting codeControlled area without public habitation
Natural growth zoneUp to 5 km radiusOnly natural population growth is permitted; the State Government controls population influx.
Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ)16 km radiusPlanning for urgent protective actions, transport and communication
Radiological Surveillance Zone (RSZ)30 km radiusEnvironmental monitoring and baseline radiological information

These are general regulatory planning criteria. The minimum exclusion-zone distance is not a claim about the exact surveyed exclusion boundary of every existing reactor, including Kakrapar.

The most important distinction between EPZ and RSZ

The 16 km Emergency Planning Zone is associated with readiness for urgent protective measures, such as communication, sheltering or evacuation when justified by an emergency.

The 30 km Radiological Surveillance Zone is associated with environmental surveillance and the collection of radiological information. It has a different purpose from the 16 km EPZ.

16 km: emergency preparedness. 30 km: radiological surveillance. Neither distance means that everyone within the corresponding circle must automatically evacuate during an incident.

Planning depends on more than distance

Effective emergency planning also considers population distribution, villages, schools, hospitals, roads, transport availability, weather, water use and other local conditions. The direction of a possible release, environmental measurements and the nature of the event influence decisions about where protective measures may be required.

A hospital or school may need special arrangements because its occupants cannot necessarily move as quickly as other members of the public. Plans must therefore identify vulnerable groups and suitable communication and assistance arrangements in advance.

Prelims focus

  • Nuclear emergencies are distinguished as plant, site and off-site emergencies.
  • Plant management primarily handles plant and site emergencies.
  • District authorities coordinate protective measures in the public domain.
  • The general EPZ radius is 16 km.
  • The general RSZ radius is 30 km.
  • Trap: An emergency-planning boundary is not an automatic evacuation boundary.

[Sources: Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Site Evaluation of Nuclear Facilities, Safety Code AERB/NF/SC/S (Rev. 1), July 2014, sections 2.2.1–2.2.4 and 5; AERB, Nuclear Power Plants, section on Emergency Preparedness and Response, consulted 16 November 2026; Government of India, National Report to the Convention on Nuclear Safety, Seventh Review Meeting, August 2016, sections 16.2.3–16.2.5; AERB, Preparedness of Operating Organisation for Handling Emergencies, Safety Guide AERB/SG/O-6, section 3.]

pictures.alt: Concentric reactor zones: minimum 1 km exclusion, up to 5 km growth control, 16 km emergency planning and 30 km environmental surveillance.
pictures.caption: Planning distances have different purposes and do not imply automatic evacuation.

title: Nuclear emergency categories and protective planning zones

body:
Why the district administration is involved

A nuclear-power station is responsible for the safety of its installation, but a possible emergency affecting the surrounding population requires action beyond the plant boundary. The district administration can mobilise public services, communicate with residents, manage movement and arrange assistance.

The District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), headed by the District Collector or District Magistrate as applicable, is responsible for coordinating disaster management in the district. In a nuclear off-site emergency, the district response works with technical information supplied by the nuclear installation and relevant specialist agencies.

For Kakrapar, the installation is in Surat district. However, planning and exercises can involve neighbouring administrative areas, including Tapi district, because a potential emergency is not restricted by district boundaries.

Who performs which function?

  • NPCIL and plant management: assess plant conditions, take protective action within the installation, classify and report abnormal conditions, and provide technical information to the authorities.
  • AERB: establishes regulatory requirements, reviews emergency preparedness and performs its regulatory functions during relevant events.
  • District administration and DDMA: coordinate public warning, local protective actions, transport, medical assistance, shelters and other district services.
  • Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA): supports the state's disaster-management planning, preparedness and coordination framework.
  • Specialist response agencies: provide technical, medical, monitoring, rescue or other assistance according to the applicable emergency plan.

Preparedness before an emergency

District preparedness is not limited to keeping a document in an office. It requires advance knowledge of the affected area's population, roads and public facilities, together with arrangements that can be activated when needed.

Important preparatory activities include:

  • Identifying settlements and vulnerable groups: villages, schools, hospitals and people who may require transport or assistance.
  • Preparing public-warning arrangements: deciding how reliable information and protective instructions will reach communities.
  • Identifying transport routes and shelters: ensuring that movement and temporary accommodation can be organised if ordered.
  • Preparing medical and monitoring support: identifying hospitals, trained responders and arrangements for radiation surveys and medical evaluation.
  • Training and conducting exercises: checking whether different organisations understand their responsibilities and can work together.

The district response must also consider other hazards. For example, an earthquake or flood may obstruct roads, damage communication systems or create additional demands on emergency services. Therefore, nuclear-emergency planning and general disaster preparedness need to be coordinated.

Gujarat's nuclear and radiological disaster action plan

GSDMA has an Action Plan for Nuclear & Radiological Disaster addressing preparedness and response for such events in Gujarat. The plan recognises Kakrapar Atomic Power Station in Surat district and the need to define responsibilities among participating organisations.

An example of preparedness: the 2026 Kakrapar exercise

GSDMA's disaster-risk-management information lists a nuclear/radiological emergency mock-drill scenario associated with an earthquake at KAPS, Surat and Tapi, dated 27 February 2026.

The entry is part of GSDMA's list of mock-drill activities. It is not evidence that an actual nuclear accident or radioactive release occurred on that date. Its significance is that the exercise scenario connects nuclear emergency preparedness with another hazard and involves more than one district.

What mock drills are meant to test

A mock drill allows agencies to practise an emergency response without waiting for a real disaster. It can reveal weaknesses in warning systems, communication, transport arrangements, interdepartmental coordination and public understanding.

After an exercise, responsible organisations can use the findings to improve plans, training and resources. Preparedness is therefore a continuing process rather than a one-time activity.

Prelims focus

  • DDMA coordinates district-level disaster management.
  • The District Collector or District Magistrate heads the district disaster-management authority as applicable.
  • GSDMA maintains Gujarat's disaster-management planning framework.
  • Kakrapar is in Surat district, while regional preparedness may involve Tapi district.
  • GSDMA lists a KAPS-related earthquake and nuclear-emergency mock-drill scenario dated 27 February 2026.
  • Trap: A mock-drill scenario is not proof of an actual nuclear disaster.

[Sources: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Action Plan for Nuclear & Radiological Disaster, introductory section, consulted 16 November 2026; GSDMA, Chapter XVII: Other Information, section 17.4, Disaster Risk Management Programme, part IV, Mock Drills, entry dated 27 February 2026, consulted 16 November 2026; Government of India, National Report to the Convention on Nuclear Safety, Seventh Review Meeting, August 2016, sections 16.2.5–16.2.6; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Site Evaluation of Nuclear Facilities, July 2014, section 5.]

pictures.caption: A preparedness exercise tests coordination among local authorities, responders and communities.

pictures.alt: A continuing cycle links district planning, training, mock drills, identifying gaps and improving plans and preparedness.
pictures.caption: Preparedness connects planning, training, exercises and improvement.
